teaser: They are not sisters, and the basket in the corner is a painter's palette in disguise.
review_notes:
Model identified as Jeanne Darlot, about 18, a future actress; the child is unidentified.
Durand-Ruel bought the canvas in July 1881 for 1,500 francs and gave it the title Two Sisters; Renoir's own title was roughly 'Woman on a Terrace by the Seine'.
Annie Swan Coburn paid $100,000 in 1925; the painting entered the Art Institute with her bequest (1933).
Painted on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise at Chatou, same location as Luncheon of the Boating Party.

lesson.text: The canvas is one meter tall and 81 centimeters wide, about 40 by 32 inches. At that size, the young woman in the red hat is close to life size. Stand in front of her in Chicago and she sits across from you like a stranger at the next table of a riverside café.

That is nearly what she was. In the spring of 1881, Renoir set up his easel on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise, a restaurant on an island in the Seine at Chatou, west of Paris. Parisians came by train to row, eat and flirt. Renoir, who had just turned 40, had spent the previous summer on this same terrace painting his big Luncheon of the Boating Party.

The two sisters are not sisters. The older girl was Jeanne Darlot, about 18, who hoped to become an actress. Nobody knows the name of the child. Renoir called the picture something like “Woman on a Terrace by the Seine.” The family title came from his dealer.

Renoir did not paint every part of this picture with the same hand. Some areas are finished as carefully as a porcelain figurine. Others are a storm of loose dabs. Compare three places and you will see how sharply he switches.

lesson.title: Three ways to paint
lesson.text: Two faces and a riverbank: watch how the brush changes from one to the next.

spots.title: A polished face
spots.text: Jeanne's skin is smooth, the strokes blended until they vanish. Her eyes and lips have clear edges. This is close to what an official portrait painter of the day would have delivered.

spots.title: The child
spots.text: The same care for the little girl: round cheeks, wet blue eyes. But she looks slightly past you, as children do when asked to hold still.

spots.title: The river
spots.text: Behind them, nothing has an outline. A rowing boat and sail boats on the Seine are a few flicks of orange and white, and the trees are scribbles of green, blue and violet.

lesson.text: So the picture has two speeds. The background is pure Impressionism: quick touches that catch the shimmer of a spring day, with no drawing underneath. The figures are slow and firm. Renoir chooses for you where your eye may rest and where it has to keep moving.
Renoir mixes two manners in one canvas: firm, smooth faces set against a background of loose, flickering strokes. The contrast is what makes the girls feel so present.

Color does the rest. The hat is the strongest red in the picture, and it sits in a sea of green. Red and green are complementary colors, meaning opposites that make each other look more intense when placed side by side. Renoir then needed somewhere to gather all his other colors together.
One object on this terrace holds every color of the painting in a single heap. Where is it?

spots.title: The basket of wool
spots.text: Balls of knitting wool: red, pink, dark blue, green, yellow. Each one is a thick swirl of pure paint. It is the picture's color chart, slipped in as a sewing basket.

lesson.text: Go back to the whole image with that basket in mind. The red of the wool returns in the hat. The dark blue is Jeanne's dress, the pink is the flowers on the child's head, the green is everywhere. The basket works like a key in the corner of a map.

The art dealer Paul Durand-Ruel bought the canvas in July 1881, only weeks after it was finished, for 1,500 francs. He showed it the following year at the seventh Impressionist exhibition, under the title he had chosen himself.
With so much flicker, the scene could fall apart. It does not. Two simple shapes hold everything in place, and once you have seen them you can feel how steady the picture is.
Two lines that organize the terrace.

lines.label: The railing
lines.text: The iron rail cuts the picture in two: the terrace below, the river and the wide world above. Jeanne's head rises over it. The child stays entirely beneath.

lines.label: The pyramid
lines.text: From the top of the red hat down to the basket on one side and the child on the other: a broad triangle, the most stable shape a painter can use.

lesson.text: A few months after this spring on the river, Renoir left for Italy. In front of the frescoes of Raphael he began to doubt the loose Impressionist touch and to long for firmer drawing. The carefully modeled faces on this terrace show that the doubt had already started.
In 1925 a Chicago collector, Annie Swan Coburn, paid 100,000 dollars for the painting. She left it to the Art Institute of Chicago, where it has hung since the 1930s.
Jeanne Darlot did go on stage. The little girl beside her walked off the terrace and out of history. She has been looked at by millions of people, and not one of them has known her name.

quiz.question: Where did Renoir paint this scene?
options: On a restaurant terrace by the Seine at Chatou
quiz.explanation: He worked on the terrace of the Maison Fournaise, on the Seine west of Paris.

quiz.question: Who gave the painting the title Two Sisters?
quiz.explanation: The dealer Paul Durand-Ruel chose the title; the models were not related.

quiz.question: What is in the basket at the lower left?
quiz.explanation: The basket holds balls of knitting wool in all the colors of the painting.

quiz.question: How do the faces differ from the background?
options: They are smooth and firm, the background is loose
They are sketchier than the background
They are painted in a single color
quiz.explanation: Renoir blended the faces carefully and left the landscape in quick, separate touches.

quiz.question: Why does the red hat look so intense?
options: It is painted with gold leaf
It is surrounded by its complementary color, green
quiz.explanation: Red and green are opposites that strengthen each other side by side.

facts.text: The two girls in the painting were sisters from Renoir's own family.
facts.explanation: They were unrelated: an 18-year-old aspiring actress and a child whose name is unknown.

facts.text: The older girl is painted close to life size.
facts.explanation: The canvas is about one meter tall, so her figure is nearly as large as a real person.

facts.text: Renoir traveled to Italy later in the same year he painted this picture.
facts.explanation: He left a few months later and came back wanting firmer drawing.
